feed.title: Venning Family Games
feed.subtitle: New games and updates on the family games hub.

entry.title: Chicken Cross — all twelve birds, redrawn
entry.summary: Redrawing the flamingo last week had an awkward side effect: it made the other eleven birds look like what they were. Underneath, every one of them was the same chicken with something bolted on — the duck was a chicken with a green head, the swan was a chicken with a black mask, the penguin was a chicken painted dark. They have all been drawn again from scratch, each with its own shape rather than its own colour. The duck is long and low with a broad flat bill and webbed feet. The penguin stands upright like a skittle with its flippers down its sides and its heels out in front. The owl is mostly face. The rooster has three green sickle feathers arching over his back, the parrot has a hooked beak and a tail that hangs past its feet, the peacock has a fan with proper eyes on it, and the swan has a long thick neck and the black knob over its bill that tells it from a goose. Nothing about the game has changed — same forty levels, same traffic, same trains, same scores — and every bird is careful to stay short enough that it never hides the lane you are about to cross.

entry.title: Block Party — somewhere for the party to happen
entry.summary: Block Party plays exactly as it did — same pieces, same eight-by-eight board, same combo streak, same Super Clear, and every best score and coin you have already earned is still there. What it has is somewhere to happen. The board used to be a rectangle floating on a flat purple screen; it is now a lit table in a party hall, with bunting strung above it, balloons drifting up the walls, confetti and streamers already fallen on the floor and glitter hanging in the light. None of that can ever get in the way of the game: every part of it is cut around the board and the tray, so a block is never hidden by decoration, even when all sixty-four squares are full. Four things that used to happen in silence now tell you something, and the important one is this: when you are holding a piece somewhere it will not fit, it now says so while you are still holding it, instead of only beeping at you once you had let go. A piece you drop somewhere impossible flies back to its tray rather than vanishing; picking one up lifts it off the table and leaves a hole behind; and setting one down lands it with a bump. A finished line gets a sweep of light down its length before it goes, a piece with nowhere left to play loses its colour and stops bobbing, and the title and results screens now draw real blocks instead of borrowing squares from your phone's emoji. Anyone who has asked their device for less movement gets a room that holds still.

entry.title: Chicken Cross — ten worlds that look like ten places
entry.summary: Chicken Cross has not changed — every level, every car, every train, every coin and every star you have already earned is exactly where you left it. It has been redrawn. The ten worlds used to be the same place in different colours: the same green tree stood on the snow, on the sand and on the volcano. Now each one has its own ground and its own things growing on it — snow-capped firs and blocks of ice, cacti and layered sandstone, palms, poplars, clipped city trees with bollards beside them, and burnt stumps on ash with cracks that glow orange. Trucks have a cab and a box instead of being long cars, logs have end grain, the train is an engine pulling two carriages, and the cars at night throw their headlights down the road ahead. Three things that used to happen in complete silence now show you something: landing a hop kicks up dust in the colour of whatever you landed on, taking a coin leaves a ghost of the coin behind, and — the important one — when the camera is creeping up behind you the bottom of the screen now warns you, which is the only death in the game you used to get no warning about at all. There is a proper menu and button system, the title screen draws whichever bird you play as, and anyone who has asked their device for less movement gets a world that holds still.

entry.title: Chicken Cross — the flamingo is a flamingo now
entry.summary: Rosalie pointed out that the flamingo you could pick as your bird just looked like a chicken painted pink, and she was completely right — underneath it was the chicken, with pink paint and very slightly longer legs. It has been redrawn from scratch as an actual flamingo: a small body carried high on stilt legs, a long curving neck, and a big pale bill that bends sharply down to a black tip. Leave it standing still for a moment and it tucks one leg up, the way they really do. Nothing about the game has changed — same levels, same traffic, same scores, and every other bird is exactly as it was — and the new one is careful to stay short enough that it never hides the cars in the lane you are about to cross.

entry.title: Tiny Rex — a valley worth looking at
entry.summary: Same hunts, same rules, same dinosaurs — Tiny Rex has just been drawn properly. The four valleys each have their own ground now rather than a flat wash of colour: grass, ferns, flowers and mossy logs in Fern Hollow, bone shards and cracked earth in Bone Gulch, scree and lichen on Spike Ridge, ash drifts and glowing cracks in Thunder Basin. The clearing sits inside a real valley, with planting leaning in over the wall and cloud shadow crossing the ground. Every animal has a shadow under it and the same inked edge, so they look like one illustrator drew the lot. Rex is jade with a cream belly so you can always find her, and she gains a stripe on her back and a spike on her crest with every size she reaches — she blinks, looks where she is going, opens her jaw when she bites and crouches before she pops up a size. Eating something leaves a ghost of it swelling and fading, growing gets a gold ribbon across the valley, and bumping noses with something your own size finally makes a friendly little squeak instead of nothing at all. The buttons, counters and cards all match now, the hearts are drawn rather than borrowed from the phone, and anyone who has asked their device for less movement gets a valley that holds still.

entry.title: Math Invaders
entry.summary: A wall of aliens is coming down, and every one of them is carrying a sum. Type an answer and the cannon fires at whichever alien that answer belongs to — so it isn't "solve this question", it's fifteen questions at once and a decision about which ones you can afford to leave. The maths you skip keeps coming, and the row you kept putting off is the one that reaches the line. Eighteen sectors run from 5 + 3 to (9 + 7) × 4, adding two-digit sums, every times table, division, negatives, powers and brackets one at a time. Get one wrong and it doesn't just buzz: the game works out which alien you meant from the mistake you made — a row out, a dropped carry, a lost minus sign, a bracket ignored — lights that one up with its answer and names what went wrong, for the cost of your chain and a moment rather than a life. Power-up pods drift down carrying little sums of their own, and answering one banks a Freeze, a Smart Bomb or a Shield to spend when you choose. Seventeen medals unlock eight ships and six skies, nothing anywhere can be bought, and Classic — endless, on Cadet, Pilot or Ace — is where the family leaderboard lives. Built for Rosalie and up, and a real game for grown-ups too.

entry.title: Brick Breaker DX — twice the game
entry.summary: The campaign runs to fifty levels now instead of thirty, and the two new worlds bring bricks that do not sit still. Circuit City has turrets that shoot back at your paddle, sliders that creep along their row, chainlinks that all take a hit when one of them breaks, and regenerators that heal themselves if you leave them alone. The Void adds ghost bricks that fade out on a cycle, so the ball goes straight through one that is not quite there. Two new bosses at the end of each: a Mainframe whose weak spots keep swapping sockets, and the Void Eye, which sheds its armour, then its tentacles, and then simply pulls your ball toward it. The three menu tiles that said "Coming soon" since the start now work — Endless waves that never stop, a Daily Challenge that is the same run for everybody who plays it that day, and a Boss Rush against all five bosses on a single set of lives. Thirteen upgrades in the shop rather than seven, twenty-seven badges to collect, and Laser Start now gives four seconds instead of eight, because eight was making levels too easy.

entry.title: Bramble Brigade
entry.summary: Five beds, one gate, and everything in the garden after your vegetables. Plant a brigade down the rows and hold the patch — Wellsprings make the water that everything else costs, Peppershots do the shooting, a Bramble simply refuses to move. Nothing stays the right answer for long: a snail's shell shrugs off ordinary shots, wasps fly clean over the ground line you just built, moles tunnel under your front row and come up behind it, and an aphid clump bursts into two when it dies. Every row has a scarecrow that saves it once. Twenty-four levels across four gardens, and each garden changes a rule rather than adding more pests — at dusk no water falls from the sky, the rockery puts stone where you wanted to build, and on the compost heap any square that loses a plant turns sour. Four bosses, a potting shed of permanent upgrades, and a Long Summer that never stops coming.

entry.title: Aquamarine
entry.summary: Two dice a turn, and you take one of them: draw a box that size onto the ocean and whatever it encloses is yours. Three dives, three air tanks and a wheel turning from day to night as you spend them, with some creatures counting only in daylight and others only after dark. Five maps, each with its own twist — caves that need a torch, a trench reached through a tunnel, ice that charges you for swimming beside it. A digital version of the print-and-play by Postmark Games, made for us rather than by them.

entry.title: Tiny Rex
entry.summary: You hatch tiny, and there is one question in the whole game: is that smaller than me? Eat it if it is, keep away if it is not, and anything exactly your own size is completely safe. Fill your belly and you grow a size, and everything you spent the last minute running from turns into dinner. Twenty hunts across four valleys, each ending on a named beast that hunts you until you out-grow it and then bolts. Stars come from your hearts and never from the clock, so you can take as long as you like. Plus the Endless Feast for the family leaderboard, and a Dino Book that fills in as you meet things.

entry.title: Curio Cabinet
entry.summary: The oldest game there is: turn over two cards, and if they match they stay open. Twenty-five halls across five wings, and each wing starts on a smaller board than the last one finished — because the difficulty comes from the cards rather than the size. Friendly animals to begin with, then shells and pressed flowers, then a Star Room where nearly everything is small and round and glowing, then a workshop of identical brass, and finally a Reading Room of numbers and capital letters with nothing to picture at all. Every board flashes face-up for a moment before the clock starts, and the look gets shorter the deeper you go. Stars come from misses rather than from the clock. Time Attack starts on thirty seconds and grows the board every time you clear it, and there is a two-player game for one table, where finding a pair means you go again.

entry.title: Updraft
entry.summary: A hot-air balloon game where you cannot steer. You have a burner and a vent, so up and down is all you control — everything sideways is decided by which of six winds you are sitting in, and they all blow different ways. The whole stack is on screen at once, because picking a layer is the game. The top wind is fastest and the air is thin enough up there that the burner drinks gas at double the rate. Rising columns lift you for free. Drop a sandbag and you leap upward, and you will never dive as fast again. Birds tear the envelope, and every tear makes it cool quicker for the rest of the flight. Twenty flights over meadows, chalk downs, a storm coast and a mountain pass, plus a Long Drift that makes one endless sky a day — the same sky for everyone in the house.

entry.title: Cookie Crumble, rebuilt
entry.summary: Cookie Crumble is a completely different game from the one that went up yesterday. It is not a cookie production line any more — it is a village tearoom floor, with an owl for a waitress. Show people to a table, take the order, put the urn and the oven on, load your tray at the pass and get it out before anybody gives up waiting. Every job is one tap; what costs you is that you have to walk there and can only be in one place. Eight animal regulars each break your routine in exactly one way, and there is an endless Saturday Rush for the leaderboard.

entry.title: Cookie Crumble
entry.summary: Run a cookie shop. Mix the dough, cut the shape somebody asked for, and be standing at the oven when the gauge hits the green stripe — a second late is crispy and five is burnt. Then ice it, add sprinkles if they wanted them, and get it to the counter before anybody gives up waiting. Your hands only hold one tray, which is the whole problem. Twenty shifts across five weeks, each ending on a Big Day, and an endless Big Rush for the leaderboard.

entry.title: Bubble & Brew
entry.summary: A push-your-luck game at an alchemist's cauldron. Draw ingredients out of your bag one at a time — each one stirs the potion higher and the points climb faster near the top, but too much fizzroot and the lid comes off and the round is gone. Stop in time, spend the coins at the apothecary, and the bag you gamble with next round is the one you just built. Twenty recipes, a bottomless cauldron for the leaderboard, and a Daily everyone plays with the identical bag.

entry.title: Wonder Museum
entry.summary: A word search with a museum wrapped round it. Fourteen wings and a hundred and twelve rooms, and every room you finish puts a real exhibit in your album with a fact on the back of it. There is a Daily Puzzle the whole family plays on the same grid.

entry.title: Number Ninja
entry.summary: Numbers fly up from the dojo floor: slice the right ones and let the rest fall. Twelve belts take the 2 to 12 times tables one at a time and then all at once, and the wrong answers are the ones people actually give, so nothing can be guessed by eye.

entry.title: Canary Deep
entry.summary: Minesweeper, a thousand feet down a coal mine, and no board here ever needs a guess. A solver plays every board through first, and any that would come down to a coin toss is thrown away. Eighteen shifts down three seams, plus a Daily Seam on the same board for everyone.

entry.title: Scribble Speedway
entry.summary: Draw a racetrack with your finger and the game turns your scribble into a real circuit, then puts seven rivals on it. Eighteen challenges across four chapters, and a Daily Circuit where the whole family gets the same field and each draws their own way round it.

entry.title: Rocket Rescue
entry.summary: Little creatures are stranded down in the caves and you have the only ship small enough to reach them. Twenty caves across four worlds, each ending somewhere a Guardian lives, plus Deep Rescue: one endless cave a day, the same one for everybody.

entry.title: Turret Town
entry.summary: They are coming up the road. Build something. Archer Posts, Bomb Lobbers, Frost Fans, Tesla Coils and Watchtowers against armour, flyers and splitters. 15 maps, three bosses, an armoury, and an endless Long Siege for the rest of us to chase.

entry.title: Ricochet Spire
entry.summary: Slay the Spire meets Breakout. Bounce a ball, break some bricks, then start drafting cards and watch it turn into something else. A branching map of battles, elites, shops, campfires and bosses, and a Daily Challenge on one seed a day. Aimed at teens and grown-ups.

entry.title: Sorting Office
entry.summary: Every parcel has a box: find it. Sort by shape, then colour, then two things at once, then by counting stamps, then by reading the label. Then the bell rings, the rule changes and every box swaps its label. No timer and nothing to lose.

entry.title: Critter Clash
entry.summary: Take your turn, there is no clock. Lead three critters against the bugs across 20 levels and three bosses, and use the garden against them: bugs cannot swim, so one good shove into the pond beats three hits. Two of you can play on one iPad.

entry.title: Word Siege
entry.summary: Hangman with a castle instead of a gallows. Every miss is a boulder through your wall, and the wall has to last the whole siege, not just one word. 18 sieges, six realms, 144 words with clues, and an armoury to spend your coins in.

entry.title: Beat Bugs
entry.summary: Tap the bugs in time with the music and watch them dance. Twelve cheerful songs from gentle two-lane tunes to fast four-lane raves. No timers and no losing, just stars to earn and more songs to unlock.

entry.title: Reel Rush
entry.summary: You have hooked a fish deep in the ocean, now reel it up to the boat. Hold to reel, slide to steer past sharks and sea mines, and stay ahead of the deep shark rising below. Land it and the next cast goes deeper for a bigger catch.

entry.title: Alien Chomp
entry.summary: You are a starving alien loose in the city. Eat every human you can to keep your hunger up, but never bite a robot. Jump, dive-slam and chomp your way from the suburbs to the spaceport.

entry.title: Deep Jungle
entry.summary: Run, jump and swim through 6 jungle worlds hunting a lost city of gold. Find secret passages, unlock explorer gear and beat the boss of every world.

entry.title: Brick Breaker DX
entry.summary: Smash neon bricks, catch power-ups and battle bosses across a 30-level campaign. Earn coins, buy upgrades and chase the family high score.

entry.title: Bible Quest
entry.summary: Journey through 17 Bible stories, from Creation to the Early Church. Answer multiple-choice questions, earn stars and unlock the next story.

entry.title: Monza
entry.summary: The classic racing dice board game, rebuilt for the web. Roll the coloured dice and steer your car around the track to the chequered flag. Two to six players.

entry.title: Chicken Cross
entry.summary: Hop your chicken across busy roads, rushing rivers and railway lines. How far can you get before the traffic gets you?

entry.title: WordVoyage
entry.summary: A word puzzle adventure around the globe. Solve puzzles, collect stars and voyage from country to country.

entry.title: Block Party
entry.summary: Drag the blocks, fill a line, make it sparkle. A gentle block puzzle made for little hands: no timer, no losing, lots of confetti.
